newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Official designs for Brazil global bond questioned.
newsitem.headline: Official designs for Brazil global bond questioned.

text.p: Economists questioned the Brazilian government's stated intention to use its new $750 million global bond to repay costly domestic debt, saying the money would likely go toward reducing Brady bond obligations.
"A global bond does not work as a substitute for domestic debt and I don't know why they keep insisting on that point," said Tomas Malaga, an economist at Unibanco bank in Brazil.
Since the Central Bank announced plans late last month to issue a global bond, it has said the funds would be used to repay part of its swelling 220 billion reais ($213.7 billion) internal debt.
Central Bank international affairs director Gustavo Franco has highlighted the point in meetings with investors ahead of Monday's launching of the five-year bond.

The logic behind the local debt retirement plan is clear. The government pays upward of 12 percent annual rates on its short-term local debt when it can borrow abroad for about nine percent with longer maturities.

Brazilian companies have actively borrowed abroad this year, taking advantage of the interest rate spread to lengthen the average maturity period on their debt. But economists say it is a little more complicated for the government.

They say bringing in dollars to retire local federal debt would disrupt the government's monetary policy - by increasing the money supply and lowering interest rates - unless the government issued even more domestic bonds to "sterilize" the dollar inflows, which would defeat the purpose of its plan.
"Under most circumstances, the Central Bank can't exchange domestic debt for external debt," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist for BMC bank in Brazil.

Allain said that if there were strong dollar outflows, due to heavy imports or the payment of foreign debt obligations, then the Central Bank could tolerate a significant inflow of dollars without issuing new domestic debt.
"That is more or less the case now. But it may not be the case a month from now and no one knows when the government's money will come into Brazil," Allain said.

Economists speculated that a more likely scenario would be that the government use the global bond funds to buy back restructured Brady bond debt on the secondary market, where it trades at a discount. They say a Brady buyback made financial and strategic sense.
Financially, Brazil would save by retiring Brady bonds at a fraction of their face value price. The buyback also would free up collateral in the form of U.S. Treasury bonds backing the Brady debt.

Brazil could also gain stategically by carrying out a swap of its Bradies for new global bonds, which trade in the market at a better price. The lower price reflects a better risk perception for Brazil as a whole, which allows the sovereign, state companies and corporations to borrow more cheaply in world debt markets, they said.
Although the Central Bank has stated publicly that it has no plans to buyback Brady debt in the near future, amny economists think it has already being doing so.
"The Central Bank has probably been buying back Brady bonds secretly and that is the best use for the money," Malaga said.
